tests.name: Z67.zero_ideal
tests.statement: If I=0, gr_I(M) is M concentrated in degree zero, over R; positive-degree pieces vanish.

tests.name: Z67.mixed_characteristic
tests.statement: For R=Z_(p), I=(p), M=R, gr_I(M) is F_p[T] with p^n mapping to T^n. No ring section F_p→R exists or is required.

tests.name: Z67.non_field_base
tests.statement: For R=k[[t]], I=(t^2), gr_I(R)≅(k[t]/(t^2))[T] with T the initial class of t^2. Replacing R/I by the residue field would give the wrong length, by a factor of two.

tests.name: Z67.finite_torsion_module
tests.statement: For R=k[[t]], I=(t), M=R/(t^q), the graded module has one-dimensional pieces in degrees 0,…,q−1 and zero thereafter; it is not a free module over gr_I(R).

uses.how: Makes the Hilbert–Samuel length function a sum of finite graded-piece lengths.
Provides the maximal-ideal special case without a residue-field section.

api.name: IdealAdicGraded.mk
api.statement: Send x∈I^n M to its degree-n class in gr_I(M).

api.name: IdealAdicGraded.mk_eq_zero
api.statement: The degree-n class of x vanishes if and only if x∈I^(n+1)M.

api.name: IdealAdicGraded.smul_mk
api.statement: The degree-i class of a∈I^i times the degree-j class of x∈I^j M is the degree-(i+j) class of ax.

api.name: IdealAdicGraded.degreeZeroEquiv
api.statement: The degree-zero piece is M/IM as an R/I-module.

api.name: IdealAdicGraded.generatorMap_surjective
api.statement: The graded polynomial-module evaluation from chosen finite ideal and module generators is surjective.

api.name: IdealAdicGraded.map
api.statement: Compatible ring, ideal and module maps induce semilinear graded maps; identity and composition are preserved.

items.name: Hilbert–Serre for finite graded modules with finite-length coefficients
items.statement: Let A be an Artinian commutative ring and N a finite N-graded module over A[X1,…,Xe], with every Xi of degree one. Put H_N(T)=Σ_n length_A(N_n)T^n. There is p∈Z[T] with H_N=p/(1−T)^e in Q[[T]], and the graded-piece lengths eventually agree with a rational polynomial. For e=0 the series is a polynomial and its eventual coefficient polynomial is zero. This is a finite-length specialization of R09.1’s general Noetherian graded Hilbert-polynomial supplier; no restriction on char(A) is imposed.
items.locator: Stacks 00K1 Proposition10.58.7 and 00K0; direct kernel/cokernel rational-series proof of the finite-length specialization, using pinned L87.
proofSteps: Replace a finite generating set by the finite collection of its homogeneous components. In each degree the module is a quotient of finitely many homogeneous polynomial pieces L96; these have finite A-length by L99. Thus every coefficient is an integer before casting to Q.
Induct on e. When e=0, the finitely many homogeneous generators and the degree-zero scalar action imply that only finitely many degrees are nonzero. This gives the polynomial numerator directly.

For e>0 set x=Xe, K=ker(x:N→N) and C=N/xN, with K carrying its unshifted inherited grading. Both are finite by L95; x annihilates both, so they are finite graded modules over A[X1,…,X_(e−1)]. The multiplication-by-x map shifts degree by one.

For each n≥0, with N_(−1)=K_(−1)=0, the exact sequence 0→K_(n−1)→N_(n−1)→N_n→C_n→0 gives l(N_n)−l(N_(n−1))=l(C_n)−l(K_(n−1)). Split at the image and apply L88 twice. Summing yields (1−T)H_N=H_C−T H_K. In particular the kernel term has a T factor; dropping it gives false coefficients for nilpotent x.

Use the induction numerators to obtain p=p_C−T p_K and denominator (1−T)^e. Apply L87 over Q. The characteristic-zero hypothesis is on Q, which receives natural lengths, and not on A. Uniqueness follows from L87. The general K0-valued or coherent-sheaf versions stay at R09.1; this local consumer does not duplicate them.
items.note: Shared supplier already promised by AlgebraicModuliForArithmeticGeometry:R09.1, whose AUDIT-01 row explicitly identifies the missing graded-module Hilbert–Serre theorem. Source addition, not a second Hilbert-polynomial owner.

tests.name: Z68.one_variable_free
tests.statement: For N=A[T] with length(A)=a, H_N=a/(1−T), so every degree has length a.

tests.name: Z68.nilpotent_generator
tests.statement: For N=k[T]/T^q, C=k in degree zero and K=k in degree q−1; (1−T)H_N=1−T^q, which detects the missing-shift error.

tests.name: Z68.positive_characteristic
tests.statement: For A=F_p, the same rational polynomial in Q counts lengths. It is not evaluated in F_p, where sufficiently large factorial denominators are unavailable.

items.name: Existence of the Hilbert–Samuel polynomial for a finite module
items.statement: Let (R,m) be Noetherian local, I a proper ideal with √I=m, and M a finite R-module. The functions h(n)=length_R(I^n M/I^(n+1)M) and χ(n)=length_R(M/I^(n+1)M) are finite and eventually rational-polynomial-valued; χ(n)=Σ_(j=0)^n h(j) for every n. Write P_(I,M) for the unique eventual cumulative polynomial. If M≠0, this polynomial is nonzero and has positive leading coefficient; if M=0 it is zero.
items.locator: Stacks 00K8 Proposition10.59.5 and 00K4 definitions; adapter from Z67/Z68 to the pinned rational-series formula.
proofSteps: R/I is Noetherian and has just one prime, m/I, so L92 makes it Artinian. Apply Z67 to gr_I(M); its finite homogeneous pieces have finite length over R/I, and L89 identifies this with their R-length.

The successive quotients in 0⊂I^n M/I^(n+1)M⊂…⊂M/I^(n+1)M and L88 give the displayed cumulative identity and finite length of every quotient. No length is cast out of N∪{∞} before this finiteness proof.

By Z68 the graded series is p/(1−T)^e. Its cumulative series is p/(1−T)^(e+1), since multiplication by Σ_(n≥0)T^n takes partial sums. L87 supplies P_(I,M) and its eventual uniqueness; this also handles e=0, when I=0 and M has finite length.

If M≠0, Nakayama L23 and I⊂m imply M/IM≠0. Hence every χ(n)≥1, so its eventual polynomial is nonzero and its leading coefficient is positive by elementary polynomial growth over Q. Do not identify its degree with dimension until Z64.

items.name: Finite-colength inclusions preserve the leading Hilbert–Samuel term
items.statement: For R,I as in Z69 and finite M with submodule M′ of finite colength l=length(M/M′), choose c with I^c M⊂M′. For n≥c, l+χ_(I,M′)(n−c)≤χ_(I,M)(n)≤l+χ_(I,M′)(n). If M′ has infinite length, P_(I,M) and P_(I,M′) have the same positive degree and leading coefficient, and their difference has smaller degree.
items.locator: Stacks 00K4 Lemma10.59.2 and 00KB Lemma10.59.9; full finite-colength squeeze.
proofSteps: A finite-length module over a local ring is annihilated by a power of m: every simple composition factor is R/m, and induction on the length multiplies the annihilators. Since I⊂m this yields the required c on M/M′.
For n≥c, I^(n+1)M⊂M′, and length additivity gives χ_M(n)=l+length(M′/I^(n+1)M). The inclusions I^(n+1)M′⊂I^(n+1)M⊂I^(n+1−c)M′ give precisely the two inequalities, with the stated shifts.

If M′ has infinite length, Z74 gives positive degree. Both bounding polynomials have the same degree and leading coefficient, since translation and addition of a constant preserve those data in positive degree. Their difference from P_M therefore has lower degree. The finite-length case must not claim strict degree drop below zero.

items.name: Exact-sequence degree comparison for Hilbert–Samuel polynomials
items.statement: Let R,I be as in Z69 and 0→M′→M→M″→0 an exact sequence of finite modules. With deg(0)=−∞, deg P_(I,M)=max(deg P_(I,M′),deg P_(I,M″)). If M′ has infinite length, the defect P_(I,M)−P_(I,M′)−P_(I,M″) has degree strictly smaller than deg P_(I,M′). If M′ has finite length, the defect is eventually zero and P_(I,M)−P_(I,M″)=length(M′).
items.locator: Stacks 00K6 Lemma10.59.3 and 00KC Lemma10.59.10, including the finite-length case.
proofSteps: Identify M′ with the injected submodule. L91 gives c and N=M′∩I^c M such that M′∩I^(n+1)M=I^(n+1−c)N for n≥c. M′/N embeds in M/I^c M, hence has finite length l.

Taking the exact quotient sequence and splitting M′/I^(n+1−c)N through M′/N gives χ_M(n)=χ_M″(n)+χ_N(n−c)+l for n≥c. This is an exact equality of finite lengths; replacing the induced filtration by I^(n+1)M′ without Artin–Rees is not valid.

If M′ has infinite length, N also does. Z70 makes P_M′−P_N lower degree. Translation makes P_N(n)−P_N(n−c) lower degree, and Z74 ensures this degree is positive so the added constant is also lower degree. Subtract the displayed identity to obtain the defect bound.

If M′ has finite length, a power of I kills N. The stabilized intersection is therefore zero for n sufficiently large, so the kernel of M/I^(n+1)M→M″/I^(n+1)M″ is exactly M′ and the difference is its length.

Nonzero cumulative polynomials have positive leading coefficients by Z69, so the degree of their sum is the maximum. The lower-degree defect cannot change this. Handle zero modules with deg(0)=−∞, which also makes the all-zero sequence correct.

tests.name: Z71.dvr_multiplication
tests.statement: For 0→k[[t]] --t→k[[t]]→k→0 and I=(t), P_R(n)=n+1 and P_k(n)=1; the defect is −1 of degree zero, strictly below degree one.

tests.name: Z71.finite_length_kernel
tests.statement: For 0→k→k⊕R→R→0, the cumulative-polynomial difference is exactly 1, and the defect after subtracting P_k is zero.

tests.name: Z71.not_exact_additivity
tests.statement: The DVR multiplication example disproves exact additivity P_M=P_M′+P_M″ for all finite modules; only the lower-degree defect theorem applies.

items.name: Independence of the Hilbert–Samuel degree from an ideal of definition
items.statement: For a nonzero finite module over a Noetherian local ring, the degree of P_(I,M) is independent of the proper ideal I with radical m.
proofSteps: For I and J choose a,b≥1 with J^a⊂I and I^b⊂J, using finite generators and equality of radicals. Then J^(a(n+1))M⊂I^(n+1)M and I^(b(n+1))M⊂J^(n+1)M.

The quotient surjections imply χ_I(n)≤χ_J(a(n+1)−1) and the reversed inequality with b. Substitute eventual polynomials; all nonzero leading coefficients are positive, and positive affine rescaling preserves degree. The two inequalities force equality of degrees. This does not assert equality of leading coefficients or polynomials.

tests.name: Z72.powers_change_multiplicity
tests.statement: For R=k[[t]], I=(t), J=(t^q), χ_I(n)=n+1 and χ_J(n)=q(n+1). Both have degree one but their leading coefficients differ when q>1.

items.name: An ideal of definition bounds cumulative growth by its generator number
items.statement: For a Noetherian local R and an ideal of definition I generated by e≥1 elements, length_R(I^n/I^(n+1))≤length_R(R/I) binom(n+e−1,e−1), and deg P_(I,R)≤e. If e=0, I=0, R is Artinian and P_(I,R) is the positive constant length(R).
items.locator: Stacks 00KQ, parameter-number-to-polynomial-degree step, with Z75 making the monomial count explicit.
proofSteps: The generator map of Z67 surjects from the degree-n homogeneous piece of (R/I)[X1,…,Xe] to I^n/I^(n+1). Z75 identifies its finite free rank as the stated binomial. Restrict scalars by L89 and use L88 to bound quotient length by source length.

Sum in degrees 0,…,n. The elementary binomial recurrence gives Σ_j binom(j+e−1,e−1)=binom(n+e,e); alternatively telescope Pascal’s identity. This is a degree-e polynomial in n with positive leading coefficient. The nonnegative eventual polynomial P_(I,R) is bounded by it and hence has degree at most e.
For e=0 there are no positive powers to count: I=0 and √0=m implies that R is zero-dimensional, so L92 makes it Artinian. The cumulative quotient is R for every n.

items.name: Degree-zero Hilbert–Samuel polynomials detect finite length
items.statement: For R,I,M as in Z69 with M≠0, deg P_(I,M)=0 if and only if M has finite length. In that case P_(I,M)=length_R(M).
items.locator: Stacks 00K4 discussion after Lemma10.59.7 and 00KI; explicit Nakayama boundary argument.
proofSteps: If P is constant, χ(n)−χ(n−1)=length(I^n M/I^(n+1)M) is zero for large n. Set N=I^n M, finite by Noetherianity. Then N=IN⊂mN⊂N, so Nakayama L23 forces N=0. M is now one of the finite-length quotients from Z69.

If M has finite length, its local composition factors are residue-field modules. Induction on the length shows m^s M=0 for some s, hence I^s M=0. Thus χ is eventually the positive constant length(M). Include the nonzero hypothesis: for M=0 the polynomial is zero, of degree −∞.

items.name: Rank of a homogeneous polynomial piece
items.statement: For a commutative ring A and e≥1 variables of degree one, the homogeneous degree-n piece of A[X1,…,Xe] is finite free on the monomials X^a with Σ_i a_i=n, a family of cardinality binom(n+e−1,e−1). With no variables the degree-zero piece is A and all positive pieces vanish.
items.locator: Stacks 00K2 Example10.58.9; monomial-basis adapter to the pinned stars-and-bars count L98.
proofSteps: A homogeneous polynomial is the finite sum of its degree-n monomials with their coefficients. Coefficient extraction proves independence of those monomials over an arbitrary coefficient ring; no division or field hypothesis is used.

Identify an exponent tuple with the multiset containing a_i copies of variable i. The total-degree condition is exactly multiset cardinality n, and the inverse records multiplicities. L98 gives the cardinality; binomial symmetry gives the displayed form when e≥1.
Treat the empty variable set directly rather than applying a formula involving e−1. The basis contains just 1 in degree zero, and has no elements in any positive degree.

items.name: A prime ideal contains a minimal prime
items.statement: For ideals I≤J with J prime in a commutative ring, there is a prime minimal over I contained in J. Use I=0 to prepend a minimal prime to a chain whose first prime is not minimal.
items.note: Statement and ambient hypotheses read at the pinned commit; no new Lean implementation.

items.name: Finite modules over Artinian rings are Artinian
items.statement: Over an Artinian ring, every finitely generated module is Artinian. Together with the Noetherian module instance in the commutative setting, L99 gives finite length.
items.note: Statement and ambient hypotheses read at the pinned commit; no new Lean implementation.

items.name: Regular ring maps and their base change
items.statement: A ring map R→Λ is regular if it is flat and for every prime p of R the fibre ring Λ⊗_R κ(p) is Noetherian and geometrically regular over κ(p), that is L⊗_{κ(p)}Λ⊗_Rκ(p) is regular for every finite extension L/κ(p). Two consequences are used here: a regular map is flat, so it satisfies going down; and for any finite type R→R′ the base change R′→Λ⊗_R R′ is again regular. Geometric regularity is strictly stronger than regularity of the fibres when κ(p) is imperfect, which is why the characteristic-p case cannot be treated by fibrewise regularity alone.
items.locator: Stacks 07BZ (Definition 15.42.1) and 07C1 (Lemma 15.42.3, regular maps and base change), read 23 September 2026
proofSteps: The definition is the flatness of R→Λ together with, for each prime p, Noetherianity and geometric regularity of Λ⊗_Rκ(p) over κ(p). Unfold geometric regularity as regularity of L⊗_{κ(p)}(Λ⊗_Rκ(p)) for every finite extension L/κ(p); over a perfect residue field this reduces to regularity of the fibre, and over an imperfect one it does not, which is the whole point of the notion.

Flatness gives going down, which is what Z77 consumes. Base change along a finite type map preserves both halves: flatness is stable under base change, and the fibre of R′→Λ⊗_RR′ over a prime q lying over p is a localisation of a finite type algebra over the fibre of R→Λ, whose geometric regularity is preserved by Stacks 07C1. This item asserts only the definition and that lemma; it does not assert that a regular map has regular source or target.

items.name: Dimension formula along a going-down map
items.statement: Let R→S be a homomorphism of Noetherian rings, q a prime of S lying over p, and suppose going down holds for R→S — for instance because R→S is flat. Then dim(S_q)=dim(R_p)+dim(S_q/pS_q). The hypothesis is going down, not flatness, and the formula is an equality of Krull dimensions of local rings, not of the rings themselves.
proofSteps: Apply the pinned height equality already recorded as L12 to p and q. The pinned localization-dimension equality identifies ht(p) and ht(q) with dim R_p and dim S_q.

Localizing S/pS at the image of q identifies it with S_q/pS_q, so the final height is the dimension of that local quotient. This is the same dimension formula, not a missing second theorem. The previous claim that neither inequality exists at the pins was incorrect.
items.note: Freshly read both declaration statements and their binders. This is an imported existing height theorem with its canonical local-dimension interpretation, not a new Lean proof. Keep L12 as the shared named supplier; Z77 is the previously assigned alias retained to avoid dangling references.

items.name: Faithfully flat descent of regularity and of Noetherianity
items.statement: Let R→S be a faithfully flat ring map. If S is Noetherian then R is Noetherian, and if S is a regular ring then R is a regular ring. The direction is descent: the hypothesis is on the target and the conclusion on the source. This does not say that regularity ascends, which is the separate statement Z59 proves under a fibre hypothesis.
items.locator: Stacks 07NG (Lemma 10.164.4, regularity) and 033E (Lemma 10.164.1, Noetherianity), read 23 September 2026
proofSteps: Noetherianity is the specialization M=R of pinned L118. For a prime p of R, faithful flatness gives a prime q of S above it.

The localized map R_p→S_q is flat and local; the target is regular local. Apply the explicit syzygy descent Z92. A resolution of κ_q cannot simply be descended as a finite free resolution of κ_p; Z92 instead begins with a resolution over R_p.

items.name: G-rings and their stability under essentially finite type maps
items.statement: A ring R is a G-ring if it is Noetherian and for every prime p the map R_p→(R_p)^∧ to the completion at the maximal ideal is regular in the sense of Z76. If R is a G-ring and R→S is essentially of finite type, then S is a G-ring. Being a G-ring is a property of the local rings, so it can be checked and used prime by prime.
proofSteps: The definition is local: R is a G-ring exactly when every R_p is, because the condition quantifies over primes and localisation of a G-ring at a prime is again one. That is what lets the finite type statement be proved one prime of S at a time.

Reduce through localizations, quotients and polynomial extensions as in the source. After the finite complete-local normalization reduction, regularity of the polynomial algebra is pinned L116 and completion regularity is Z96. For characteristic zero use the corrected two-case fibre proof Z99: a nonzero prime requires a quotient by a separable polynomial and the derivation criterion. The positive-characteristic geometric-regularity arguments in 07PR/07PU and the Cohen-structure reduction remain an explicit source/declaration audit frontier.
